However, more and more of that clean energy is also going to waste. In order to balance energy supply and demand, electric utilities rely on a process called curtailment, where they deliberately reduce the amount of energy produced by solar and wind farms in order to not overwhelm the energy grid. But a new MIT study asks: what if that excess clean energy could be used to power some of the United States’ dirtiest sectors? While solar and wind energies are essential to achieving decarbonization goals and avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, their intermittency introduces new challenges and complexity to energy markets and infrastructure. The production patterns of these renewable energy sources are often at odds with demand patterns. The sun is setting on solar farms just as families are returning home and firing up their appliances. And during the day, when production is at its highest, demand slumps. One of the most key approaches to this problem is energy storage , which can hold onto excess energy produced at peak hours and release it back onto the grid when demand outstrips supply. However, the energy storage sector is still in its infancy and battery storage can only hold onto energy for about four hours at a time. Long-term energy solutions, while very promising, are still in research and development stages and are not commercially viable or scalable. It would therefore be most efficient to divert that excess energy production to where it actually is needed – manufacturing and data centers. The idea of diverting clean energy to where it’s needed isn’t new, but it has lacked the infrastructure and data to reliably be carried out. “The key challenge is how to harness that extra energy, sending it to places where demand is high, or storing it for still and sunless days,” reads a Zenobe report . “At present, we don’t have sufficient network infrastructure to achieve this. This means that high levels of renewable generation put pressure on the grid, and sometimes even risk overloading it. At such times, the ESO safeguards the grid by paying generators to stop producing electricity,” Zenobe goes on to say. “This drives up bills for consumers, and wastes precious renewable energy.” But it’s not just an issue of infrastructure. It’s also an issue of being able to reliably model when and where that excess energy will be available in order to design systems around it. A new study from MIT and Georgia Tech, published this week in the energy-focused scientific journal Joule , seeks to answer that need. The study models the future of wind and solar growth the the United States. Specifically, the study looks at the amount of excess energy to be produced as the domestic renewable sector continues to develop, and the patterns of when that excess energy will be produced. “The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available,” explains a recent article from MIT News. “It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.” These models are based on a point in the future clean energy development wherein 80 percent of the electricity supplied to United States consumers is coming from solar and wind power. The Middle East conflict in late February changed that outlook. Rising energy and transportation costs threatened to push inflation higher across the economy. By late March, expectations of rate cuts had largely disappeared. Then came another complication: the US labor market remained resilient. Unemployment stayed between 4.1% and 4.3% over the spring and summer, giving the Federal Reserve greater flexibility to fight inflation. The evolution of the Fed’s own economic projections illustrates how dramatically the outlook changed. November brought a particularly aggressive shift in market expectations. Investors now anticipate three additional quarter-point rate increases by June 2027, including December’s expected hike. Higher interest rates make government bonds and other interest-bearing investments more attractive while increasing the cost of borrowing. title: Alphabet's AI Spending Under the Microscope as Credit Hedges Set Records - ad-hoc-news.de
body: Investors in Alphabet are being pushed to look past the headlines this week. A record reading in the credit-default swap market, an unconfirmed report of trimmed chip orders and a pair of legal developments have all landed within days of each other — and each one, on closer inspection, says less about Alphabet's prospects than the questions it raises about the return on its artificial intelligence spending. The cost of insuring against an Alphabet default climbed to a record on Wednesday for five-year contracts, according to Reuters, which noted that premiums for Oracle, SpaceX and CoreWeave also touched all-time highs. The agency tied the moves to investor unease over AI outlays and how they are financed. That concern has been building. Axios reported on 23 November that analysts had not raised their forecasts for further investment by Alphabet and other large cloud providers after the earnings season — a break from a pattern of repeated upgrades to AI spending expectations. On Tuesday, Alphabet and other AI-linked stocks came under pressure as investors questioned whether returns would justify the heavy data-center buildout. The week's most eye-catching item was an unconfirmed media report suggesting Google could cut orders for custom AI chips for 2027 by roughly 20%. On its own, such a reduction would prove neither greater efficiency nor weaker demand. Order volume says nothing about how overall capital needs will develop, nor about the revenue Alphabet can wring from existing capacity. What matters for the stock is whether additional capital translates into additional earnings. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Alphabet? The unchanged analyst forecasts are a separate matter from any company decision. Axios reported on expectations, not on reduced investment budgets. A forecast that stops rising merely front-runs one more increase; it does not answer whether Alphabet can extract more from its AI investments. In the best case, Google needs fewer additional chips without any deterioration in its AI revenue outlook — a lower need for new silicon that sits comfortably alongside a better return. But that would require more than confirmation of a smaller order: Alphabet would also have to show the reduced need does not stem from weaker business prospects. A favorable scenario does not depend on a cut at all; even with spending still high, the company could demonstrate that extra capacity pays off. For investors, a statement on expected revenue relative to investment needs would carry more weight than any single order number. The counter-risk is that fewer orders signal softer demand while data-center expansion costs stay elevated. A purchasing cut would then offer scant offset to diminished revenue prospects — and even if the rumor never confirms, the risk remains that earnings fail to keep pace with the investment tempo. Financing sensitivity was on display in a Bloomberg Law report from 19 November: two energy prepayment deals totaling $3 billion were delayed amid weak investor demand and market volatility. Alphabet should still receive the funds, and the delay does not prove any cutback in AI investment. It does, however, explain why investors should watch the financing of individual projects alongside planned spending. The next concrete test would be a confirmation or denial of the reported 2027 orders. A confirmation alone would not settle which scenario applies — the reason would be decisive. Does Google need less additional capacity because it can use existing capacity better, or because it expects less business? A denial, meanwhile, would clear the rumor without answering whether AI revenue justifies the capital deployed. Alphabet at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. body: St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation. During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity. "The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said. Musalem said the real policy rate, which subtracts the inflation rate from the Fed's target rate, needs to be between 2%-2.5% by next spring, and estimated that the current rate is about a full point below that range. That position suggests the Fed may need to hike at each of the upcoming Fed meetings in December, January, March and April. Musalem does not get a vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee over the period where he says that the rate increases will be needed, though he does get to present views and provide input on the "dot plot" of individual members' expectations. He will next vote in 2028. To be sure, Musalem noted "an unlikely but still plausible scenario" in which no further hikes would be needed. "Falling energy prices and lower shipping costs, or an increase in potential output growth driven by higher productivity growth, might ease inflation pressures such that inflation moves toward target in 18 months," he said. Another possibility is that demand might decelerate as spending on artificial intelligence slows. "We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses , but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed. With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend. It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island. Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said. Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse believes Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) could eventually reach $1 million. That is about 16.7 times its current price of $59,763. Bitcoin trades 52.6% below its all-time high of $126,080 reached on October 6, 2025, and has lost 22.9% in November alone. Over the past month, it has swung between $81,274 on October 28 and $58,818 on November 20. The decline has run for more than a year. Market analyst Charlie Bilello noted on November 21 that Bitcoin’s 56% drop from its October 2025 peak has lasted 411 days, the longest peak-to-trough decline in Bitcoin’s history. So how high could Bitcoin’s price go in 2035? Market cap is a coin’s price multiplied by the number of coins in circulation. About 20.1 million Bitcoins are in circulation, which is roughly 96% of the total cap of 21 million. At $1 million per coin, that works out to about $20.1 trillion, against Bitcoin’s market value of about $1.2 trillion. With the end of 2035 roughly 9.1 years away, Bitcoin would need to grow about 36% a year to hit that market cap. Our November 22 analysis tests whether Bitcoin can still reach $1 million based on its past performance. Supply growth also affects price comparisons over time. When Bitcoin closed at $8,118 on November 22, 2017, the network’s market value was around $135.5 billion. Another halving is projected for around 2032, which may slow new supply before it reaches the 21 million cap. Halvings also squeeze miners, since each one halves their reward. Brent crude climbed to $96.61 per barrel , while U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) advanced to $85.79 per barrel , recovering part of the ground lost since October highs. Market sentiment shifted sharply following repeated reports of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi strikes targeting Saudi energy infrastructure, including areas near the Ras Tanura export hub and Red Sea ports. Recent export data also shows that energy commodity shipments from the Middle East remain below pre-war levels, with liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports running at roughly half their pre-conflict pace. These figures directly contradict earlier International Energy Agency projections that anticipated a global supply glut based on September export rebounds. With no diplomatic breakthrough between the United States and Iran, actual crude flows have fallen back from September and October peaks. Commodity strategists note that persistent physical supply constraints could push prices even higher. Support for the Euro (EUR) comes from a weaker US Dollar (USD) and the hawkish message in the account of the European Central Bank’s (ECB) October meeting. Data published after the September meeting had bolstered the argument for tighter policy, leaving many ECB policymakers willing to support an October rate rise, according to minutes released on Thursday. Nevertheless, the decision to hold rates steady was unanimous. Members preferred a measured approach in light of tighter financial conditions, downside risks to economic growth and the absence of material second-round effects from rising energy prices. October’s core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation rate climbed to 3.3% YoY, the quickest pace since late 2023. Meanwhile, an upward revision took third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth from an annualised 3.4% to 4.3%. That gives the Fed greater scope to increase rates with fewer concerns about a slowdown in growth. Further uncertainty stems from Washington’s proposed new round of tariffs on imports from China, the European Union and other major trading partners. Based in Frankfurt, Germany, the European Central Bank (ECB) serves as the Eurozone’s reserve bank, setting the region’s interest rates and conducting its monetary policy. Maintaining price stability is the ECB’s principal mandate, meaning it aims to keep inflation at around 2%. Adjusting interest rates up or down is its main means of doing so. Higher relative interest rates generally strengthen the Euro, while lower rates tend to weaken it. Monetary policy is decided by the ECB Governing Council, which meets eight times a year. The decision-makers are the heads of the Eurozone’s national central banks and six permanent members, among them ECB President Christine Lagarde. When circumstances are extreme, the European Central Bank can turn to Quantitative Easing, a policy tool known as QE. Under this approach, the ECB prints Euros to purchase assets from banks and other financial institutions, usually government or corporate bonds. The Euro typically weakens as a result. Used as a last resort, QE is intended for situations in which interest rate cuts alone are unlikely to deliver price stability. Once an economic recovery is under way and inflation begins to rise following QE, the central bank can move to its opposite: Quantitative tightening (QT). title: Finance Minister Blames Fed Rate Outlook as Rupiah Slips Past 18,400 - Jakarta Globe
body: Jakarta. Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara on Thursday attributed the rupiah’s mounting pressure to robust US economic growth and rising inflation, which have fueled expectations of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve and raised the prospect of capital outflows from emerging markets. The Indonesian currency briefly weakened past Rp 18,400 against the US dollar earlier in the day before recovering to around Rp 18,300. Suahasil said the strength of the US economy, coupled with rising inflation, had increased the likelihood of monetary tightening by the Fed, potentially drawing more international capital into the United States. “The US economy is growing very strongly. In addition to strong economic growth, inflation is also rising,” Suahasil told reporters in Jakarta. He said the prospect of higher US interest rates had become a major concern for global investors because of its potential impact on international capital flows. “The US central bank has consistently said it will seek to maintain stability. One of its policy options is to raise interest rates, and that is what the entire world is watching,” Suahasil said. He added that expectations of monetary tightening alone could prompt investors to shift their funds to the United States in anticipation of more attractive returns, even before the Fed takes any action. “If the United States raises interest rates, or even before it actually does so, expectations alone can cause capital to move toward the United States,” Suahasil said. Higher US interest rates could intensify capital outflows from emerging markets, including Indonesia, as dollar-denominated assets become more attractive to global investors. Such a shift could weaken demand for rupiah-denominated assets and put further pressure on the Indonesian currency. Bank Indonesia Governor Destry Damayanti previously said the rupiah had depreciated by 9.54% since the beginning of 2026, reaching Rp 18,195 per dollar on November 23. The central bank also expects the Fed could raise its benchmark interest rate by 25 to 50 basis points in December, highlighting the external challenges facing Indonesia’s currency stability.

title: US economy roars ahead in Q3; inflation remains high in October | Gulf Times - Gulf Times
body: The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. The sharp upward revision to gross domestic product last quarter, reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, marked the quickest economic growth pace in three years. It reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment, mostly related to artificial intelligence. Robust domestic demand is fueling inflation, with a measure of underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-over-year increase since late 2023. The economy has powered ahead despite the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. "It is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "It was once thought that import tariffs and energy prices from the Mideast war were one-off factors behind the higher inflation numbers, but increasingly the inflation fires look to be stoked by old-fashioned economic demand pressures." GDP increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. It was the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2023. The economy was previously estimated to have grown at a 3.4% pace. Economists polled by Reuters had expected GDP growth to be revised up to a 3.5% pace. The economy grew at a 2.2% rate in the April-June quarter. Related Story 'US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to consider leaving Opec' US consumers seen spending despite inflation woes Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate. That was the strongest pace since the fourth quarter of 2024 and was an upgrade from the previously reported 3.8% pace. Spending is being driven mostly by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market before the ongoing AI-led selloff. Economists expect consumer spending to slow to a still-healthy pace in the fourth quarter, though declining gasoline prices should ease some of the financial pressure on middle- and lower-income households. Average retail gasoline prices have dropped below $4 a gallon for the first time since mid-July, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed. Disposable household income, adjusted for taxes and inflation, rebounded in October, and the saving rate increased after declining for two straight months, the BEA said in another report. Low layoffs, with first-time claims for state unemployment benefits at a 57-year low, are also expected to help underpin spending. The personal consumption expenditures price index measures changes in the prices of goods and services purchased by households. It differs from a simple comparison of prices for a fixed shopping basket because expenditure weights can change as consumer behaviour evolves. The Federal Reserve uses this measure in assessing its longer-term inflation objective. The latest release shows that the increase in prices over the preceding year remains above the desired pace, both when all expenditure categories are included and when food and energy are excluded. The core measure excludes food and energy because their prices can be particularly volatile. This does not mean those expenses are unimportant to households. Rather, the measure provides an additional way to investigate whether price pressure is more persistent across the rest of the economy. If underlying inflation remains elevated, a temporary fall in fuel or food prices may not be sufficient to establish that broader price stability is returning. Policymakers therefore examine headline and core inflation together, rather than treating one as a substitute for the other. body: Anthropic ( ANT +10.98% ) went public on Nov. 19 at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion in one of the largest initial public offerings ever. After a wild first week, in which the stock opened at $111.50 and later closed below its offering price, it finished Friday at $91.88, about 11% above its IPO price. Wall Street's analysts have been weighing in, and so far they're pretty bullish. Wedbush rated the stock outperform with a $120 price target. Canaccord rated it a buy with a $135 target. Oppenheimer is among the highest, with an outperform rating and a $150 target, roughly 63% above current levels. One detail makes those calls more interesting than usual: none of the three firms is named anywhere in Anthropic's prospectus, which lists 22 banks on its cover. Analysts at a deal's underwriters tend to start coverage with positive ratings, but these three had no apparent direct role in the offering. The bull case starts with growth that's hard to find anywhere else among AI stocks . According to its prospectus, Anthropic's revenue rose from $1.4 billion in the third quarter of 2025 to $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026. Multiply that latest quarter by four, and the company is running at nearly $68 billion a year in sales. The analysts' argument is that this is still early. Canaccord said it is "increasingly convinced that the opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Software that completes tasks on its own can be paid for from the money companies spend on people, a far larger pool than the money they spend on software. Wedbush pointed to the "global knowledge wage pool" as the prize. Oppenheimer's target is built on a forecast of $275.1 billion in revenue in 2028, with operating margins above 20%. The business is also less dependent on a handful of big buyers than you might expect. No customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and about 79% of third-quarter revenue came from customers outside the top five. Three things in the filing deserve a hard look before you buy. First, profits are uneven. Anthropic earned an operating profit of $974 million in the second quarter of 2026, then slipped back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter as computing costs jumped 77% to $9.9 billion. (Its far larger reported net losses mostly reflect accounting charges on convertible securities.) Second, the spending commitments are enormous. Anthropic says it has signed up for about $900.9 billion of spending commitments, substantially all of it for computing and infrastructure, with $451.6 billion expected before the end of 2030 and $70.7 billion due within 12 months of Sept. 30. That next-year bill is roughly equal to its current annual revenue pace. Many of these contracts require payment whether or not the capacity gets used, so if demand cools, the costs won't shrink with it. Third, the valuation already assumes a lot. With about 13.2 billion shares outstanding after the IPO, Anthropic is worth roughly $1.2 trillion, or about 18 times its annualized revenue. To grow into Oppenheimer's 2028 forecast, revenue would need to roughly quadruple from today's pace in about two years. If you believe AI will take on a growing share of white-collar work, Anthropic is one of the most direct ways to own that trend, and its growth so far supports the analysts' optimism.
